historical_timeline.summary: Born in New Rochelle, New York.
Breast enlargement (gynecomastia) in adolescence, as he later described it.
Finds a lump under the left nipple; biopsy shows breast cancer.
Mastectomy (single or double, accounts differ) with spread to the lymph nodes; then six months of chemotherapy.
Speaks publicly about his breast cancer for the first time.
Describes in a television interview his embarrassment at the diagnosis and the lasting numbness under his left arm.
Died at his home in Los Angeles, aged 81.

claims.statement: Richard Roundtree was born on July 9, 1942, in New Rochelle, New York.

source_links.locator: Early life section, citing the Los Angeles Times obituary

claims.statement: Roundtree was an actor best known as the private detective John Shaft in films beginning in the early 1970s, and is described as the first Black action hero.

Roundtree told PEOPLE that at the end of September 1993, in the shower, he felt a lump under his left nipple, 'the size of a lima bean'; he was not overly concerned at first, because at 13 he had had gynecomastia (breast enlargement), and he 'just chalked it up to that.'
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own public account; the attribution of a new lump to earlier gynecomastia is the delay the synthetic episode teaches against.

source_links.locator: PEOPLE interview as republished in October 2023

claims.statement: In a 2019 television interview Roundtree said he found the lump in the shower while working in Costa Rica in 1993 and saw his doctor after returning to Los Angeles a week later; the doctor biopsied it and four or five days later told him he had breast cancer. Asked whether he had felt shame, he answered 'Embarrassment,' and he said men 'are so cavalier about their health issues and want to sweep it under the rug.'
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account of the stigma. It adds a location and a week's gap that the PEOPLE account does not give; the two are not in conflict on the diagnosis.

claims.statement: Roundtree told PEOPLE that his physician called him four or five days after the visit to tell him in person; that a day or two later he was in the hospital for a modified radical mastectomy, which removed the complete breast from the sternum to the underarm, including the nipple and areola; and that the cancer had spread to the lymph nodes. The same article describes the operation as removing his left breast.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account of a single-sided operation on the left. See CLM-0006 for the conflicting reports.

source_links.locator: PEOPLE interview as republished in October 2023

claims.statement: Sources differ on the extent of the operation: his own account in PEOPLE describes a modified radical mastectomy of the left breast, while the Associated Press obituary and an encyclopedia article (citing a 2001 USA Today interview) say he underwent a double mastectomy.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The conflict is recorded and not resolved. Neither account is preferred, and the synthetic record does not settle whether the right breast was removed.

source_links.locator: Title-level record of the 2001 interview; not read

claims.statement: Roundtree said that after the operation he had six months of chemotherapy, that he lost 18 pounds, and that 'the nausea is something you never, ever forget.'
claims.clinical_interpretation: Treatment he made public; the regimen was not made public.

source_links.locator: PEOPLE interview as republished in October 2023

claims.statement: Roundtree said he kept his treatment secret for fear it would end his film career, keeping his undershirt on during the physical examinations required for each film; that 'nobody ever knew I was even in the hospital'; that about six years after treatment, when he had been given the all-clear, he decided to speak up, telling PEOPLE in 2000; and that he was 'not embarrassed,' urging men to speak about breast cancer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The secrecy and the later advocacy at the center of the teaching on stigma.

source_links.locator: PEOPLE interview as republished in October 2023

claims.statement: In the 2019 interview he said that the left side of his chest had no feeling under the arm.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A lasting effect he described publicly; numbness under the arm after axillary surgery is common.

claims.statement: Roundtree died at his home in Los Angeles on October 24, 2023, aged 81; his longtime manager said he had been diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only. The pancreatic cancer is not part of the synthetic episode, and no link to the breast cancer is asserted.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Men get breast cancer. Evaluate a new breast lump in a man of 51 promptly, without accepting an earlier history of gynecomastia as an explanation: examination that tells a firm, eccentric cancer from soft, central gynecomastia, same-week diagnostic mammography and ultrasound of both breasts and both axillae, and core biopsy of the mass and any abnormal node; ER, PR, and HER2 status; germline genetic testing and counseling for every man with breast cancer; surgical planning with a breast surgical oncologist; lymphedema prevention; and preparation for chemotherapy followed by tamoxifen, the preferred endocrine therapy for men, on the ASCO male breast cancer guideline, the NCCN breast guideline, and the CMID breast cancer monograph. His own public account of embarrassment and of keeping his treatment secret frames the teaching on the stigma that delays men's care.

documentation.chief_complaint: Biopsy results for a left breast lump

hpi.narrative: Mr. Roundtree returns six days after first coming in with a painless lump under the left nipple. Diagnostic mammography and ultrasound of both breasts and both axillae the next day showed a 1.6 cm irregular mass eccentric to the left nipple and one abnormal left axillary lymph node; the right breast and axilla were normal. Core biopsies of the mass and the node the same day show invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 3, estrogen receptor 95 percent, progesterone receptor 85 percent, HER2 negative, with cancer in the node. He was asked to come in so the result could be given in person. He says he had not thought a man could get breast cancer and had been sure it was the breast enlargement he had at 13. He has no bone pain, cough, headache, abdominal pain, or weight loss. He saw Dr. Siddiqui of breast surgical oncology this morning, and the operation is booked in two days. His main worries are the operation, whether he can keep working, and keeping the diagnosis private.

documentation.chief_complaint: Review two weeks after left breast cancer surgery

hpi.narrative: Mr. Roundtree returns thirteen days after mastectomy with level I and II axillary dissection for left breast cancer. He went home the next day. The drain was removed on the eighth day, and the wound has healed without infection or fluid. He took acetaminophen for the first ten days and needs nothing now. He has numbness under the left arm, as he was warned, and some tightness when he lifts the arm, which is improving with the exercises. He has no arm swelling. The pathology shows a 1.6 cm grade 3 invasive ductal carcinoma with clear margins, and 2 of 15 lymph nodes involved, the largest 7 mm, with no spread through the node capsule: stage IIA (pT1c pN1a). He saw medical oncology four days ago. They advised doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide every three weeks for four cycles, then weekly paclitaxel for twelve weeks, about six months in all, starting in about two weeks, then tamoxifen for at least five years, and a radiation oncology review after chemotherapy. An echocardiogram is booked this week. The germline result is not back. He feels low at times and worries about losing his hair and about work, but he is sleeping and eating.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Roundtree is a 51-year-old man with stage IIA, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative left breast cancer, treated by mastectomy and axillary dissection three weeks ago, who comes for his periodic preventive visit before chemotherapy starts next week. The scar is healed and he has nearly full movement of the left shoulder; the numbness under the left arm is unchanged. His echocardiogram four days ago was normal. The germline test result is not back yet. He is sleeping well, is back at the gym with light lower-body work, and has told only a few close friends about the diagnosis. He no longer needs pain medicine and has no fever, cough, or bone pain.

referral.question: Man of 51 with a new 1.5 cm firm, painless lump eccentric to the left nipple and a palpable left axillary node; breast cancer suspected. Diagnostic mammography, ultrasound, and core biopsy are booked for tomorrow. Please see him as soon as the results are back to plan surgery
referral.urgency: Urgent suspected-cancer pathway, within one week
referral.pertinent_history: He found the lump in the shower a few days ago and at first put it down to the breast enlargement he had at 13. Examination: a 1.5 cm firm, irregular, non-tender mass eccentric to the left nipple at 2 o'clock, not fixed to the chest wall, with no nipple retraction or discharge; one firm, mobile 1 cm left axillary node; the right breast has no mass and no glandular enlargement. The findings are those of a cancer, not gynecomastia, which is usually soft, rubbery, central, and often on both sides. He is otherwise well, takes no regular medicines, never smoked, and drinks two or three times a week. No family history is recorded. He is an actor and is anxious that the diagnosis stay private. PHQ-2 score 1
questions: If the biopsy confirms cancer, what is the clinical stage, and does he need staging scans before surgery?
What operation do you recommend for the breast, and how should the axilla be managed if the node is positive?
Should germline testing be done before surgery, and would its result change the operation?
What should he expect after surgery, including drains, shoulder movement, and lymphedema prevention?
Who will plan treatment after surgery, and when?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Roundtree is seen at the request of Dr. Carrington. A few days before his first visit he found a painless lump under the left nipple in the shower and thought at first that it was the breast enlargement he had as a boy. Diagnostic mammography and ultrasound of both breasts and both axillae five days ago showed a 1.6 cm irregular retroareolar mass on the left and one abnormal left axillary node, with a normal right breast and axilla. Core biopsies of both show invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 3, ER 95 percent, PR 85 percent, HER2 1+, Ki-67 30 percent, with metastatic carcinoma in the node. He has no bone pain, cough, headache, or weight loss. He is fit, trains most days, and works as an actor. He says he did not know a man could get breast cancer, and he is worried about privacy at work
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Diagnostic mammography and ultrasound of both breasts and both axillae; core biopsy pathology of the breast mass and the axillary node with ER, PR, HER2, and Ki-67; today's preoperative blood count and chemistry, all normal

exam.finding: Well; anxious but composed

assessment.display: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, clinical stage IIA (cT1c cN1 M0), ER and PR positive, HER2 negative, grade 3
assessment.assessment: Men get breast cancer. In men it is usually retroareolar, as here, and usually hormone receptor-positive. He has early, operable disease with a biopsy-proven axillary node. Staging scans are not recommended for clinical stage IIA without symptoms or abnormal blood tests. Because the tumor is small and hormone receptor-positive, surgery first is reasonable; chemotherapy before surgery was discussed as an alternative, and surgery first gives the full pathology to guide treatment afterwards. With so little breast tissue in men, mastectomy is the usual operation, and with a biopsy-proven node, a level I and II axillary dissection is standard

Germline testing should be offered to every man with breast cancer. BRCA2 is the gene most often found. A variant would raise the risk of a new cancer in the other breast and of prostate and pancreatic cancer, and would matter for his relatives. It need not delay surgery, because the operation on the cancer side is the same either way

He feels embarrassed by a breast cancer diagnosis and fears it could cost him work. These are common reasons men delay care or keep it secret. He came in promptly, which is the right thing, and his care can be kept confidential

recommendations: Left total mastectomy with level I and II axillary lymph node dissection in two days

Removal of the other breast is not needed for cancer control; some men choose it for symmetry, and that choice is his. It does not need to wait for the germline result. Reconstruction is possible but rarely chosen by men; offered
No staging CT, bone scan, or PET before surgery
Genetic counseling and a germline multigene panel (BRCA2, BRCA1, PALB2, CHEK2, ATM, and others), sent today
Measure both upper arms before surgery as the lymphedema baseline
After surgery: a drain for about a week, shoulder exercises from the first day, numbness under the arm is expected, and lymphedema risk reduction for the left arm

Medical oncology after the pathology, to plan chemotherapy and endocrine therapy; tamoxifen is the first-choice endocrine therapy for men. Radiation oncology review if two or more nodes, or other high-risk features, are found
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Carrington today. The patient agrees with the plan and asked for his records to be kept confidential; written information about breast cancer in men was given
consultant_note.follow_up: Operation in two days. Surgical review of the wound and pathology in about ten days. Medical oncology after the pathology. Primary care continues distress screening and preventive care before treatment
